cards.q: Which chemical buffer system does most of the buffering in extracellular fluid?
cards.a: The bicarbonate buffer system.
options: The phosphate buffer system
The bicarbonate buffer system
The hemoglobin buffer system
The ammonia buffer system
cards.explanation: Bicarbonate is present in plasma at about 24 mEq/L, far more than any other buffer outside cells, and both of its members are under active control. Phosphate is only about 1 to 2 mEq/L in plasma, so it matters much more inside cells and in urine. Hemoglobin is a powerful buffer but it is locked inside the red blood cell. Ammonia is made by the kidney tubule and buffers urine, not plasma.

cards.q: Which member of the bicarbonate buffer system is controlled by the lungs?
cards.a: Carbon dioxide.
options: Plasma albumin
Carbon dioxide
Bicarbonate ion
Phosphate ion
cards.explanation: Ventilation sets how fast carbon dioxide leaves the body, so the lungs control the acid member of the pair. Bicarbonate is the base member and is handled by the kidney. Phosphate and albumin belong to other buffer systems entirely and are not part of the bicarbonate pair. Having one member on a respiratory dial and the other on a renal dial is exactly what makes this system so useful.

cards.q: Which member of the bicarbonate buffer system is controlled by the kidneys?
cards.a: Bicarbonate ion.
options: Carbon dioxide
Carbonic anhydrase
Bicarbonate ion
Dissolved oxygen
cards.explanation: The kidney reclaims filtered bicarbonate and can generate new bicarbonate, so it sets the base member of the pair. Carbon dioxide is the acid member and is set by ventilation. Carbonic anhydrase is the enzyme that speeds the reaction, not a buffer component that gets adjusted. Dissolved oxygen has no acid or base role in this system.

cards.q: What is the normal concentration of bicarbonate in arterial plasma?
cards.a: About 24 mEq/L.
options: About 40 mEq/L
About 4 mEq/L
About 12 mEq/L
About 24 mEq/L
cards.explanation: Normal plasma bicarbonate runs 22 to 26 mEq/L, so 24 is the value to carry. About 4 mEq/L is closer to normal plasma potassium, a number students often swap in. A value near 12 mEq/L would be a marked metabolic acidosis. A value near 40 mEq/L would be a marked metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Which plasma protein does most of the protein buffering in blood plasma?
cards.a: Albumin.
options: Albumin
Hemoglobin
Fibrinogen
Transferrin
cards.explanation: Albumin is by far the most abundant plasma protein, and its histidine side chains accept and release H+ near blood pH. Hemoglobin is an excellent buffer but it sits inside the red blood cell, not in plasma. Fibrinogen and transferrin are present in much smaller amounts and contribute little buffering.

cards.q: Which protein does most of the buffering inside the red blood cell?
cards.a: Hemoglobin.
options: Albumin
Phosphate
Hemoglobin
Carbonic anhydrase
cards.explanation: Hemoglobin is present at very high concentration inside the erythrocyte and its histidine residues accept H+ generated when carbon dioxide is hydrated. Albumin does the same job but in plasma, not inside the cell. Phosphate is an inorganic buffer and is important intracellularly, but hemoglobin dominates in the red cell. Carbonic anhydrase is the enzyme producing the acid, not the buffer absorbing it.

cards.q: Which buffer system forms titratable acid in the tubular fluid of the kidney?
cards.a: The phosphate buffer system.
options: The albumin system
The hemoglobin system
The bicarbonate system
The phosphate system
cards.explanation: Filtered phosphate accepts secreted H+ in the tubule and is excreted as dihydrogen phosphate, which is what titratable acid means. Bicarbonate in the tubule is reclaimed rather than excreted, so it carries no acid out of the body. Albumin is not filtered in appreciable amounts. Hemoglobin stays inside red blood cells and never reaches tubular fluid.

cards.q: How quickly do chemical buffers begin to limit a pH change after acid enters the blood?
cards.a: Within seconds.
options: Within 6 to 12 hours
Within 2 to 3 days
Within seconds
Within 10 to 30 minutes
cards.explanation: Chemical buffering is a reaction between molecules already present, so it works in seconds and is the first line of defense. Ten to thirty minutes is closer to the time the respiratory response needs to reach its full effect. Six to twelve hours is when the renal response becomes measurable. Two to three days is how long the kidney needs to finish compensating.

cards.q: The phosphate system has a pKa of 6.8, much closer to blood pH than the 6.1 of the bicarbonate system. Why is bicarbonate still the stronger plasma buffer?
cards.a: Plasma holds far more bicarbonate, and the lungs and kidneys adjust both of its members.
options: Plasma holds far more bicarbonate, and both are regulated
The pKa of bicarbonate rises to 7.4 once albumin is present
Phosphate stays in plasma and cannot reach the tissues
Phosphate cannot bind a hydrogen ion at 37 C
cards.explanation: Buffer power depends on concentration as well as pKa, and plasma carries roughly 24 mEq/L of bicarbonate against 1 to 2 mEq/L of phosphate, while ventilation and the kidney can move each member on demand. Phosphate binds H+ perfectly well at body temperature, which is why it dominates inside cells where its concentration is high. The pKa of a buffer pair is a property of the chemistry and albumin does not change it. Phosphate is freely filtered and distributed, so confinement is not the issue.

cards.q: A load of fixed acid enters the blood. What happens to plasma bicarbonate and to carbon dioxide before the lungs respond?
cards.a: Bicarbonate falls and carbon dioxide rises.
options: Bicarbonate falls and carbon dioxide rises
Bicarbonate rises and carbon dioxide falls
Both bicarbonate and carbon dioxide rise
Both bicarbonate and carbon dioxide fall
cards.explanation: The added H+ combines with bicarbonate to make carbonic acid, which breaks down to water and carbon dioxide, so the base is consumed and the gas accumulates until ventilation clears it. Bicarbonate cannot rise while it is being spent on the acid load. Carbon dioxide cannot fall, because it is the product of the buffering reaction. Both falling would require an entirely different disturbance, such as hyperventilation on top of the acid load.

cards.q: Which sequence gives the correct time course of the three defenses against an acid load?
cards.a: Chemical buffering in seconds, ventilation in minutes, the kidney over days.
options: Ventilation in seconds, buffering in minutes, the kidney over days
Buffering in seconds, ventilation in minutes, the kidney over days
The kidney in seconds, buffering in minutes, ventilation over days
Buffering in seconds, the kidney in minutes, ventilation over days
cards.explanation: Buffers are already dissolved in the fluid, so they act instantly; ventilation must be driven by chemoreceptors and takes minutes to reach full effect; the kidney must change transporter and enzyme activity, which takes hours to days. Ventilation cannot beat a chemical reaction that needs no signaling. The kidney is always the slowest of the three, never the fastest. Reversing the last two puts the slow organ ahead of the fast one.

cards.q: Why does buffering a fixed acid with bicarbonate depend on normal lung function?
cards.a: The carbon dioxide produced must be exhaled or the reaction stops moving.
options: The lungs deliver the oxygen that binds the excess hydrogen ion
The lungs manufacture the bicarbonate used in the reaction
The lungs supply the carbonic anhydrase for the reaction
The carbon dioxide produced must be exhaled or buffering stalls
cards.explanation: Each H+ buffered turns into a molecule of carbon dioxide, and if that gas accumulates the equilibrium pushes back and the buffer loses its power. The kidney, not the lung, makes bicarbonate. Carbonic anhydrase is inside cells such as the erythrocyte and the tubule cell rather than being supplied by the lung. Oxygen does not bind H+ and plays no part in the buffering reaction.

cards.q: Blood reaches a systemic capillary and hemoglobin releases its oxygen. What happens to its ability to buffer H+?
cards.a: It increases, because deoxyhemoglobin is a better proton acceptor.
options: It falls, because the cell loses carbonic anhydrase activity
It falls, because oxygen is needed to hold H+
It increases, because deoxyhemoglobin accepts H+ more readily
It is unchanged, because buffering does not depend on oxygen binding
cards.explanation: Deoxygenated hemoglobin is a weaker acid than oxygenated hemoglobin, so it picks up H+ more readily exactly where carbon dioxide is being loaded, which is the Haldane effect. Oxygen is not required for proton binding; releasing it is what improves binding. Saying nothing changes misses the coupling between the two gases that makes the red cell so efficient. Carbonic anhydrase content does not change as hemoglobin unloads oxygen.

cards.q: A patient's plasma albumin falls to half its normal value. What happens to the buffering power of plasma?
cards.a: The non bicarbonate buffering power of plasma falls.
options: Bicarbonate buffering rises to compensate exactly
Buffering is unchanged because albumin is not a buffer
Buffering rises because more free H+ can reach bicarbonate
The non bicarbonate buffering power of plasma falls
cards.explanation: Albumin supplies most of the protein buffering in plasma through its histidine side chains, so losing half of it removes a real share of the total buffer capacity. Bicarbonate concentration is set by the kidney and does not automatically rise to cover the loss. Albumin is very much a buffer, which is why low albumin also lowers the measured anion gap. More free H+ reaching bicarbonate means a larger pH swing, not better buffering.

cards.q: Why can the kidney excrete far more acid when phosphate is present in the tubular fluid?
cards.a: Buffered H+ does not lower urine pH as much, so secretion can continue.
options: Buffered H+ keeps urine pH from falling, so secretion continues
Phosphate is converted to bicarbonate inside the tubule cell
Phosphate raises the number of H+ ATPase pumps in the membrane
Phosphate carries H+ across the luminal membrane by symport
cards.explanation: The H+ pumps stall once urine pH reaches about 4.4, and a buffer soaks up secreted H+ so the free concentration stays low and the gradient stays workable. Phosphate does not carry H+ across the luminal membrane; the H+ ATPase and the Na+/H+ exchanger do that. Phosphate is not converted into bicarbonate, although trapping H+ on phosphate does let the cell add new bicarbonate to the blood. Pump number is regulated by acidosis and hormones, not by the amount of filtered phosphate.

cards.q: Equal amounts of acid are added to a sealed tube of bicarbonate solution and to the blood of an intact person. Which shows the smaller fall in pH, and why?
cards.a: The intact person, because the carbon dioxide formed is exhaled.
options: The sealed tube, because none of its bicarbonate is lost to urine
The intact person, because the carbon dioxide formed is exhaled
Both fall equally, because the chemistry of the buffer is the same
The sealed tube, because its temperature stays constant
cards.explanation: In the body the system is open at the lung end, so the carbon dioxide produced by buffering is blown off and the reaction keeps running forward, which is why an open bicarbonate system outperforms its pKa. In the sealed tube the carbon dioxide accumulates, the equilibrium backs up, and pH falls further. Urinary bicarbonate loss is far too slow to matter over the seconds this comparison covers. Temperature is not what separates the two systems here.

cards.q: Why is the bicarbonate system a poor buffer for a rise in carbon dioxide itself?
cards.a: It raises H+ and bicarbonate together, so the ratio still falls.
options: It raises H+ and bicarbonate together, so the ratio still falls
Carbon dioxide is a base rather than an acid in this reaction
Carbon dioxide inactivates carbonic anhydrase at high partial pressure
Bicarbonate cannot accept a hydrogen ion once carbon dioxide is high
cards.explanation: Hydrating carbon dioxide produces one H+ and one HCO3- from the same molecule, so the base cannot mop up the acid it just created, and pH is set by the ratio of the two. That is why proteins, especially hemoglobin, do the real buffering of a respiratory acid load by taking up the H+ and leaving the bicarbonate free. Carbonic anhydrase is not inactivated by high carbon dioxide. Bicarbonate still binds H+ chemically; the problem is bookkeeping, not chemistry. Carbon dioxide behaves as the acid member of the pair.

cards.q: A sustained acid load continues for several hours. Where does a large share of the buffering shift, and what electrolyte change follows?
cards.a: Into cells and bone, with K+ moving out of cells into plasma.
options: Into red blood cells only, with Cl- moving out of plasma
Into filtered phosphate only, with Na+ falling in plasma
Into cells and bone, with K+ moving out of cells into plasma
Into plasma proteins only, with Ca2+ falling in plasma
cards.explanation: Over hours H+ enters cells and is taken up by intracellular proteins and phosphate, and bone carbonate releases base as well, and to keep charge balanced K+ leaves the cell, which is why chronic acidosis tends to raise plasma potassium. Plasma proteins act within seconds and are saturated long before hours pass. Red cells help immediately but cannot absorb a sustained load on their own, and the chloride shift belongs to carbon dioxide transport, not to a fixed acid load. Filtered phosphate is a urinary buffer and does not pull sodium out of plasma.

cards.q: Arterial PCO2 rises acutely from 40 to 80 mmHg, and over the next few minutes plasma bicarbonate rises only from 24 to 26 mEq/L. What produced that small rise?
cards.a: Hydration of carbon dioxide, with H+ taken up by proteins.
options: New bicarbonate generated by the proximal tubule within minutes
Hydration of carbon dioxide, with H+ taken up by proteins
Release of stored bicarbonate from red blood cell granules
Reduced loss of bicarbonate in sweat and gastric secretions
cards.explanation: Extra carbon dioxide is hydrated to H+ and HCO3-, and because hemoglobin and other proteins take up the H+, the bicarbonate is left behind and measured concentration edges up by roughly 1 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise. The kidney cannot generate meaningful new bicarbonate in minutes, which is exactly why this rise is so small. Red blood cells store no bicarbonate granules. Sweat and gastric losses of bicarbonate are trivial and far too slow to explain a change over minutes.

cards.q: Which enzyme speeds the combination of carbon dioxide and water to form carbonic acid?
cards.a: Carbonic anhydrase.
options: Carboxypeptidase
Bicarbonate synthase
Carbonic anhydrase
Carbonic dehydrogenase
cards.explanation: Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes the hydration of carbon dioxide, and it is abundant in red blood cells and renal tubule cells where the reaction has to run fast. Carbonic dehydrogenase and bicarbonate synthase are not real enzymes of this pathway. Carboxypeptidase is a protein digesting enzyme from the pancreas and has nothing to do with acid base handling.

cards.q: What is the normal value for arterial PCO2?
cards.a: About 40 mmHg.
options: About 40 mmHg
About 60 mmHg
About 100 mmHg
About 24 mmHg
cards.explanation: Arterial PCO2 normally sits between 35 and 45 mmHg, so 40 is the anchor value. A value near 24 is the number for plasma bicarbonate in mEq/L, which is easy to confuse with a gas pressure. About 60 mmHg would be marked carbon dioxide retention. About 100 mmHg is the normal figure for arterial PO2, not PCO2.

cards.q: What is the normal range for arterial pH?
cards.explanation: Arterial pH is held in the narrow band of 7.35 to 7.45, and the midpoint 7.40 is the reference for deciding which side of neutral a compensated blood gas sits on. Values from 7.20 to 7.35 are acidemic, not normal. Values from 7.00 to 7.20 are severe acidemia. Anything above 7.45 is alkalemia.

cards.q: What happens to arterial PCO2 during hyperventilation?
cards.a: It falls.
options: It rises and then falls below normal
It rises
It falls
It stays constant while PO2 falls
cards.explanation: Hyperventilation means alveolar ventilation exceeds the rate at which metabolism makes carbon dioxide, so the gas is cleared faster than it is produced and arterial PCO2 falls. A rise in PCO2 is the mark of hypoventilation. PCO2 cannot stay constant while ventilation changes, since it is set by the balance of production and removal. There is no transient rise before the fall.

cards.q: Arterial PCO2 rises. Which way does plasma pH move?
cards.a: It falls.
options: It rises
It falls
It rises then returns to 7.40
It does not change until bicarbonate changes
cards.explanation: Carbon dioxide is hydrated to carbonic acid, which dissociates and adds H+ to the blood, so more carbon dioxide always means a lower pH. A rise in pH would require carbon dioxide to fall or bicarbonate to rise. Nothing returns pH to 7.40 without compensation over hours. Bicarbonate does not have to change first, because the carbon dioxide itself supplies the H+.

cards.q: Where are the central chemoreceptors that respond to a rise in blood carbon dioxide?
cards.a: In the medulla oblongata.
options: In the carotid bodies
In the medulla oblongata
In the aortic arch
In the pulmonary capillaries
cards.explanation: Central chemoreceptors sit on the ventral surface of the medulla and sense the H+ of cerebrospinal fluid, which tracks arterial PCO2 because carbon dioxide crosses the blood brain barrier freely. The carotid bodies and the aortic bodies are the peripheral chemoreceptors and respond mainly to low PO2. Pulmonary capillaries carry blood past the alveoli but contain no chemoreceptors.

cards.q: Which stimulus do the central chemoreceptors actually detect?
cards.a: The H+ concentration of cerebrospinal fluid.
options: The bicarbonate concentration of plasma
The H+ concentration of cerebrospinal fluid
The temperature of arterial blood
The partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
cards.explanation: Carbon dioxide crosses into cerebrospinal fluid and is hydrated there, and it is the resulting H+ that the medullary receptors sense, so they read carbon dioxide indirectly. Arterial oxygen is monitored by the peripheral chemoreceptors instead. Plasma bicarbonate and H+ cross the blood brain barrier poorly, which is why a metabolic disorder stimulates ventilation less directly than a respiratory one. Temperature affects ventilation but is not the chemoreceptor stimulus.

cards.q: How long does the respiratory response to an acid load take to reach its full effect?
cards.a: Minutes.
options: Twelve hours
Three days
Milliseconds
Minutes
cards.explanation: Chemoreceptors fire within seconds and ventilation is fully adjusted in a matter of minutes, which makes the lung the second line of defense after chemical buffers. Milliseconds is the time scale of an action potential, not of a ventilatory adjustment. Twelve hours and three days describe the renal response, which is far slower but far more complete.

cards.q: A student breathes rapidly and deeply for two minutes during an anxiety episode. Predict the changes in PCO2 and pH.
cards.a: PCO2 falls and pH rises.
options: PCO2 falls and pH rises
PCO2 falls and pH falls
PCO2 rises and pH falls
PCO2 rises and pH rises
cards.explanation: Blowing off carbon dioxide faster than it is made lowers arterial PCO2, removes acid from the blood, and drives pH up, which is respiratory alkalosis. PCO2 and pH move in opposite directions for a respiratory problem, so falling PCO2 with falling pH is not possible from hyperventilation alone. Rising PCO2 with falling pH describes hypoventilation, the opposite disturbance. Rising PCO2 with rising pH breaks the chemistry in both directions.

cards.q: A person takes a sedative that slows the respiratory rate. Predict what happens to arterial PCO2 and pH.
cards.a: PCO2 rises and pH falls.
options: PCO2 rises and pH falls
PCO2 and pH both stay normal
PCO2 falls and pH rises
PCO2 rises and pH rises
cards.explanation: Less ventilation lets metabolically produced carbon dioxide accumulate, and the extra carbonic acid drives pH down, which is respiratory acidosis. Falling PCO2 would require more ventilation, not less. A rise in PCO2 can never raise pH, because carbon dioxide is the acid member of the buffer pair. Values cannot stay normal while carbon dioxide production continues and removal has slowed.

cards.q: Adding carbon dioxide to blood shifts the reaction CO2 + H2O to H2CO3 to H+ plus HCO3- in which direction, and what happens to bicarbonate?
cards.a: To the right, and bicarbonate rises slightly.
options: To the right, and bicarbonate rises slightly
To the right, and bicarbonate falls slightly
To the left, and bicarbonate rises slightly
To the left, and bicarbonate falls slightly
cards.explanation: Extra reactant pushes the equilibrium toward products, so both H+ and HCO3- are produced and measured bicarbonate rises a little even though pH is falling. The reaction cannot run to the left when carbon dioxide is being added. Bicarbonate cannot fall while it is being generated by the same reaction. This is also why a rising bicarbonate on a blood gas does not automatically mean a metabolic alkalosis.

cards.q: Alveolar ventilation doubles while carbon dioxide production stays the same. What happens to arterial PCO2?
cards.a: It falls to roughly half its previous value.
options: It stays the same because production is unchanged
It falls to roughly half its previous value
It falls by roughly 10 percent
It doubles
cards.explanation: Arterial PCO2 is set by carbon dioxide production divided by alveolar ventilation, so doubling the denominator with the numerator fixed roughly halves the value, taking 40 mmHg toward 20 mmHg. A ten percent fall would need only a small change in ventilation. PCO2 doubles when ventilation is halved, not doubled. Unchanged production is precisely why the ventilation change is free to move PCO2.

cards.q: Why does hyperventilation raise pH even though it also lowers plasma bicarbonate?
cards.a: Carbon dioxide falls proportionally more, so the ratio rises.
options: A lower bicarbonate raises pH all by itself
Bicarbonate does not affect pH, only carbon dioxide does
Carbon dioxide falls proportionally more, so the ratio rises
The lost bicarbonate is replaced by phosphate within seconds
cards.explanation: pH tracks the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide, and hyperventilation cuts the denominator sharply while the numerator drifts down only slightly, so the ratio and the pH both rise. Bicarbonate certainly affects pH; it is the base member of the pair. Phosphate is present at far too low a plasma concentration to replace bicarbonate. A fall in bicarbonate by itself lowers pH, which is why the reasoning has to be about the ratio.

cards.q: A patient breathes into and out of a closed paper bag. Which change explains the fall in pH that follows?
cards.a: Rebreathed carbon dioxide raises arterial PCO2.
options: Slower airflow reduces carbonic anhydrase activity
The bag lowers inspired oxygen and produces lactic acid
Rebreathed carbon dioxide raises arterial PCO2
The bag raises tidal volume and clears bicarbonate
cards.explanation: Rebreathing returns exhaled carbon dioxide to the alveoli, the alveolar to blood gradient shrinks, arterial PCO2 climbs, and pH falls, which is why the maneuver was used against hyperventilation. Oxygen does drop somewhat but not enough in a short trial to produce meaningful lactic acid. Bicarbonate is not cleared by the lungs at all. Carbonic anhydrase activity is not altered by how fast air moves.

cards.q: Which chemoreceptor group produces most of the ventilatory response to a modest rise in arterial PCO2?
cards.a: The central chemoreceptors of the medulla.
options: The carotid bodies
The central chemoreceptors of the medulla
The aortic bodies
Stretch receptors in the airway wall
cards.explanation: Roughly two thirds to three quarters of the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide comes from the medullary receptors, because carbon dioxide crosses into cerebrospinal fluid readily and generates H+ there. The carotid and aortic bodies respond to carbon dioxide as well but contribute the smaller share, and their dominant stimulus is a low PO2. Airway stretch receptors regulate the depth and timing of a breath, not its chemical drive.

cards.q: A climber arrives at 4000 meters. Low PO2 drives hyperventilation. Trace the effect on PCO2, then on pH, then name the disorder.
cards.a: PCO2 falls, pH rises, and the result is respiratory alkalosis.
options: PCO2 falls, pH rises, and the result is respiratory alkalosis
PCO2 falls, pH falls, and the result is metabolic acidosis
PCO2 rises, pH rises, and the result is metabolic alkalosis
PCO2 rises, pH falls, and the result is respiratory acidosis
cards.explanation: Hypoxia stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors, ventilation increases, carbon dioxide is cleared faster than it is produced so PCO2 falls, and losing that acid drives pH above 7.45, which is a respiratory alkalosis. Rising PCO2 would need hypoventilation, the opposite of the hypoxic response. A metabolic label would require the primary change to be in bicarbonate, but here the primary change is in a gas. Nothing in this sequence raises bicarbonate.

cards.q: A student hyperventilates for one minute, then holds their breath as long as possible. What happens to pH across the two phases?
cards.a: It rises above normal during hyperventilation, then falls back through normal during the breath hold.
options: It stays constant, then falls sharply
It rises during both phases
It falls, then rises above normal
It rises, then falls back through normal
cards.explanation: Blowing off carbon dioxide first drives PCO2 down and pH up, then during the breath hold metabolism keeps making carbon dioxide with no route out, so PCO2 climbs and pH falls back toward and past normal. The order cannot be reversed, since hyperventilation always comes first here. pH cannot stay constant while PCO2 is changing. It cannot rise in both phases, because a breath hold retains acid rather than removing it.

cards.q: A patient in metabolic acidosis hyperventilates. Why can this respiratory compensation never return pH fully to 7.40?
cards.a: The falling PCO2 removes the very stimulus driving the extra ventilation.
options: Bicarbonate rises as PCO2 falls and cancels the benefit
Carbonic anhydrase is saturated once ventilation doubles
The lungs cannot lower PCO2 below 35 mmHg under any circumstance
The falling PCO2 removes the stimulus driving the extra ventilation
cards.explanation: Ventilation increases because H+ and carbon dioxide stimulate chemoreceptors, so as pH climbs back toward normal the drive weakens and ventilation levels off short of full correction, which is why compensation is fast but incomplete. PCO2 can certainly go well below 35 mmHg; values in the twenties are common in severe metabolic acidosis. Bicarbonate falls slightly rather than rising when PCO2 drops. Carbonic anhydrase has enormous spare capacity and does not become the limiting step.

cards.q: Alveolar ventilation is halved in a sedated patient whose arterial values started at pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L. Predict the new PCO2 and the direction of pH.
cards.a: PCO2 near 80 mmHg with pH well below 7.35.
options: PCO2 near 80 mmHg with pH above 7.45
PCO2 near 40 mmHg with pH unchanged
PCO2 near 20 mmHg with pH above 7.45
PCO2 near 80 mmHg with pH below 7.35
cards.explanation: PCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation at constant production, so halving ventilation roughly doubles PCO2 from 40 to about 80 mmHg, and with bicarbonate still near 24 mEq/L the ratio collapses and pH falls to roughly 7.10. A PCO2 near 20 mmHg would follow from doubling ventilation, not halving it. A high PCO2 with a high pH is chemically impossible without a large rise in bicarbonate, which cannot happen in minutes. PCO2 cannot stay at 40 when removal has been cut in half.

cards.q: Which tubule segment reclaims most of the filtered bicarbonate?
cards.a: The proximal convoluted tubule.
options: The thin descending limb
The distal convoluted tubule
The collecting duct
The proximal convoluted tubule
cards.explanation: Roughly 80 to 85 percent of filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed in the proximal tubule, which is built for high capacity bulk reabsorption. The thin descending limb is permeable to water and handles no bicarbonate transport. The distal tubule and collecting duct recover only the small remainder and are where fine adjustment of acid excretion happens, not bulk reclamation.

cards.q: Which transporter moves H+ into the proximal tubule lumen in exchange for Na+?
cards.a: The sodium hydrogen exchanger.
options: The chloride bicarbonate exchanger
The sodium potassium ATPase
The sodium hydrogen exchanger
The sodium glucose cotransporter
cards.explanation: The Na+/H+ exchanger on the luminal membrane uses the inward sodium gradient to push H+ out into the lumen, which is secondary active transport. The Na+/K+ ATPase sits on the basolateral membrane and creates that gradient rather than secreting H+ itself. The sodium glucose cotransporter carries glucose, not H+. The chloride bicarbonate exchanger moves bicarbonate out of the cell on the basolateral side and does not secrete acid into the lumen.

cards.q: Which cell of the collecting duct secretes H+ into the tubular fluid during acidosis?
cards.a: The type A intercalated cell.
options: The type A intercalated cell
The type B intercalated cell
The macula densa cell
The principal cell
cards.explanation: Type A intercalated cells carry an H+ ATPase on the luminal membrane and send new bicarbonate back to the blood, so they are the acid exporters. Principal cells handle sodium, potassium, and water under aldosterone and ADH. Type B intercalated cells are the mirror image and secrete bicarbonate during alkalosis. The macula densa senses tubular sodium chloride for tubuloglomerular feedback and does not transport acid.

cards.q: Which cell secretes bicarbonate into the tubular fluid during alkalosis?
cards.a: The type B intercalated cell.
options: The principal cell
The type B intercalated cell
The mesangial cell
The type A intercalated cell
cards.explanation: The type B intercalated cell has its pumps and exchangers arranged in reverse, so it puts bicarbonate into the lumen and H+ back into the blood, which is how the kidney corrects an alkalosis. The type A cell does the opposite and is active in acidosis. Principal cells are not acid base cells. Mesangial cells sit in the glomerulus and regulate filtration surface area.

cards.q: Which amino acid do proximal tubule cells break down to make ammonium for acid excretion?
cards.a: Glutamine.
options: Arginine
Histidine
Glycine
Glutamine
cards.explanation: Glutamine is taken up by the proximal tubule and metabolized to two ammonium ions and the carbon skeleton that yields new bicarbonate for the blood. Glycine and arginine are not the substrates for renal ammoniagenesis. Histidine is the buffering side chain in proteins, which is a different acid base role entirely.

cards.q: What are the two main urinary buffers that let the kidney excrete large amounts of acid?
cards.a: Phosphate and ammonia.
options: Albumin and hemoglobin
Phosphate and ammonia
Sulfate and lactate
Bicarbonate and chloride
cards.explanation: Filtered phosphate accepts H+ to form titratable acid, and ammonia made in the tubule cell traps H+ as ammonium, and together they carry the bulk of the daily acid load out in the urine. Bicarbonate in the tubule is reclaimed rather than excreted, so it removes no net acid. Albumin and hemoglobin never reach tubular fluid in meaningful amounts. Sulfate and lactate are anions in urine but are not significant H+ acceptors at urine pH.

cards.q: How long does full renal compensation for an acid base disorder take?
cards.a: Two to three days.
options: Two to three minutes
One to two hours
Two to three days
Two to three weeks
cards.explanation: Renal compensation begins within hours but takes two to three days to reach its full effect, because it depends on changes in transporter number and enzyme activity. Minutes is the time scale of the respiratory response. One to two hours is enough for the kidney to start but not to finish. Weeks overstates it; the kidney is slow but not that slow.

cards.q: In what chemical form does filtered bicarbonate actually cross the luminal membrane of the proximal tubule cell?
cards.a: As carbon dioxide.
options: As carbonic acid on a channel
As ammonium bicarbonate
As bicarbonate ion on a symporter
As carbon dioxide
cards.explanation: Secreted H+ combines with filtered bicarbonate in the lumen to form carbonic acid, brush border carbonic anhydrase splits it to water and carbon dioxide, and the gas diffuses into the cell where the reaction is reversed. The luminal membrane has no bicarbonate symporter for this purpose. Carbonic acid is short lived and does not cross on a channel. Ammonium bicarbonate is not a transported species here.

cards.q: A patient has been acidotic for two days. Predict what has happened to renal H+ secretion and to ammonium production.
cards.a: Both have increased.
options: H+ secretion decreased and ammonium production increased
Both have increased
Both have decreased
H+ secretion increased and ammonium production decreased
cards.explanation: Acidosis upregulates the luminal Na+/H+ exchanger and H+ ATPase and also induces the enzymes of glutamine metabolism, so the kidney both pumps more acid and supplies more ammonia to carry it out. Both falling is the response to alkalosis, not acidosis. The two processes are regulated together because H+ secretion is useless without a buffer to trap it, so a split answer in either direction misses how the system is coupled.

cards.q: A patient has a metabolic alkalosis that has lasted three days. What is the kidney doing with bicarbonate?
cards.a: Excreting bicarbonate in the urine, making it alkaline.
options: Holding bicarbonate constant while excreting more chloride
Reclaiming all filtered bicarbonate and generating more
Excreting bicarbonate in the urine, making it alkaline
Converting bicarbonate to ammonium for excretion
cards.explanation: With plasma bicarbonate high, the filtered load exceeds what the proximal tubule can reclaim and type B intercalated cells actively secrete bicarbonate, so the urine turns alkaline and plasma bicarbonate is dragged back down. Reclaiming and generating more bicarbonate is the acidosis response and would worsen the alkalosis. Bicarbonate is not converted into ammonium; ammonium comes from glutamine. Chloride excretion alone would not correct the base excess.

cards.q: A drug inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule. Predict the effect on urine and on plasma.
cards.a: Bicarbonate is lost in urine and plasma bicarbonate falls.
options: Bicarbonate is lost in urine and plasma bicarbonate falls
Urine turns strongly acidic and plasma pH rises sharply
Ammonium excretion rises and plasma pH rises sharply
Bicarbonate is retained and plasma bicarbonate rises
cards.explanation: Without carbonic anhydrase the lumen cannot break down carbonic acid, bicarbonate reclamation stalls, the alkaline urine carries base out of the body, and a metabolic acidosis develops. Retention of bicarbonate is what happens when the enzyme is working normally. The urine becomes more alkaline, not more acidic, since bicarbonate is left behind in it. Plasma pH falls rather than rises, which is exactly why this class of drug is used to blunt the alkalosis of altitude.

cards.q: Secreted H+ combines with a filtered bicarbonate ion in the lumen. How much new bicarbonate has been added to the blood?
cards.a: None, because a bicarbonate was merely preserved.
options: One new bicarbonate ion for each H+ that is secreted
Two new bicarbonate ions for each H+ secreted
None, because a bicarbonate was merely preserved
None, because the secreted H+ is reabsorbed unchanged
cards.explanation: Titrating filtered bicarbonate is reclamation, so the blood ends where it started, and net new bicarbonate is added only when secreted H+ is trapped by phosphate or ammonia and leaves the body. Counting one new bicarbonate per secreted H+ confuses reclamation with generation, which is the single most common error in this topic. Two is not the stoichiometry of any step here. The H+ is not reabsorbed unchanged; it is consumed making carbon dioxide and water.

cards.q: Why does the minimum urine pH of about 4.4 limit how much free H+ the kidney can excrete?
cards.a: Free H+ is still a tiny fraction of the acid load.
options: Free H+ is still a tiny fraction of the acid load
Tubule cells cannot survive a lower urine pH
Carbonic anhydrase stops working below that pH
The H+ ATPase reverses direction and reabsorbs acid
cards.explanation: A urine pH of 4.4 corresponds to only about 0.04 mEq of free H+ per liter, which is trivial next to a daily acid load near 70 mEq, so nearly all of the excreted acid must ride out bound to phosphate or ammonia. The H+ ATPase stalls against the gradient rather than reversing. Tubule cells are not destroyed at that urine pH; it is a normal daily occurrence. Carbonic anhydrase is not what sets this limit.

cards.q: Aldosterone secretion rises. Predict the effect on H+ handling by the collecting duct.
cards.a: H+ secretion increases.
options: H+ secretion is unchanged but bicarbonate secretion rises
H+ is reabsorbed instead of secreted
H+ secretion increases
H+ secretion decreases
cards.explanation: Aldosterone stimulates the H+ ATPase of type A intercalated cells and increases sodium reabsorption by principal cells, which leaves the lumen more negative and pulls H+ out, so excess aldosterone can produce a metabolic alkalosis. A fall in H+ secretion is the response to too little aldosterone. Bicarbonate secretion by type B cells is not the aldosterone response. There is no mechanism for reabsorbing free H+ across the collecting duct.

cards.q: Why is renal compensation more complete than respiratory compensation even though it is far slower?
cards.a: The kidney removes acid from the body altogether.
options: The kidney works much faster once it gets started
The kidney removes acid from the body altogether
The kidney is not limited by carbonic anhydrase
The kidney changes pH without changing bicarbonate
cards.explanation: Excreting H+ on phosphate and ammonia and adding new bicarbonate physically removes the acid load, and the kidney keeps working until pH is near normal because its drive does not switch off as quickly as chemoreceptor drive does. Renal compensation is slower than respiratory compensation at every stage, not faster. Carbonic anhydrase limits neither system in practice. The kidney acts precisely by changing bicarbonate, so it cannot alter pH while leaving bicarbonate alone.

cards.q: A patient with chronic lung disease has had a PCO2 near 60 mmHg for several years. Predict plasma bicarbonate and urine pH.
cards.a: Bicarbonate is high and the urine is acidic.
options: Bicarbonate is high and the urine is alkaline
Bicarbonate is high and the urine is acidic
Bicarbonate is low and the urine is alkaline
Bicarbonate is normal and the urine is alkaline
cards.explanation: Years of carbon dioxide retention drive the kidney to secrete H+ and generate new bicarbonate, so plasma bicarbonate climbs into the thirties while the acid leaving in the urine keeps urine pH low. A low bicarbonate would make the acidemia worse rather than compensating for it. A normal bicarbonate would mean no compensation at all, which is not possible after years. Alkaline urine would mean the kidney was dumping the very bicarbonate it needs to retain.

cards.q: A patient has vomited gastric contents for three days and is now volume depleted with a metabolic alkalosis. Why does the kidney keep reabsorbing bicarbonate rather than excreting it?
cards.a: Volume depletion drives sodium reabsorption, and H+ secretion follows.
options: Vomiting removes the enzyme needed for bicarbonate secretion
A high plasma pH directly inhibits glomerular filtration
The kidney cannot excrete bicarbonate at any plasma concentration
Volume depletion drives sodium reabsorption, and H+ follows
cards.explanation: Low volume raises angiotensin II and aldosterone, both of which stimulate the Na+/H+ exchanger and the H+ ATPase, so the kidney keeps secreting acid and reclaiming bicarbonate and the urine stays acidic even in alkalosis, which is why restoring volume is what lets the alkalosis resolve. The kidney can normally excrete bicarbonate very effectively; that ability is being overridden here. Vomiting removes gastric acid and fluid, not renal enzymes. Filtration is not directly shut down by a high plasma pH.

cards.q: A climber takes a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor before ascending. Trace the effect through the kidney to arterial pH and explain why it helps at altitude.
cards.a: Bicarbonate is lost in urine, lowering pH and offsetting alkalosis.
options: Bicarbonate is lost in urine, lowering pH and offsetting alkalosis
Ammonium excretion falls, raising plasma pH and blunting the hypoxia
H+ secretion rises, lowering plasma pH and slowing ventilation down
Bicarbonate is retained, raising plasma pH and deepening each breath
cards.explanation: Blocking the enzyme stops proximal bicarbonate reclamation, base is lost in an alkaline urine, plasma bicarbonate and pH fall, and that mild metabolic acidosis counteracts the respiratory alkalosis caused by hypoxic hyperventilation so ventilation can stay high. Retaining bicarbonate would raise pH and suppress the very drive the climber needs. Ammonium excretion changes are not the main mechanism and would not lower pH. H+ secretion falls rather than rises when carbonic anhydrase is inhibited, and the goal is more ventilation, not less.

cards.q: A patient develops a metabolic acidosis this morning. Compare what has happened by ten minutes and by three days.
cards.a: Ventilation rises in minutes, and the kidney corrects pH over days.
options: Ventilation rises in minutes, and the kidney corrects pH over days
Nothing changes for three days, when ventilation finally rises
Ventilation rises only after the kidney has finished at three days
Renal bicarbonate generation finishes in minutes, so pH is normal by ten minutes
cards.explanation: Chemoreceptors drive hyperventilation within minutes, which lowers PCO2 and limits the fall in pH but cannot fully correct it because the drive fades as pH improves; over two to three days the kidney excretes the acid load and regenerates bicarbonate, bringing pH close to normal. The kidney cannot generate meaningful bicarbonate in minutes. Something does change immediately, since buffering and then ventilation both act early. The order is fixed by the machinery involved, so ventilation cannot wait on the kidney.

cards.q: What term describes an arterial pH below 7.35?
cards.a: Acidemia.
options: Hypoxemia
Alkalemia
Acidemia
Hypercapnia
cards.explanation: Acidemia is the measured state of blood that is too acidic, and it is the first thing to read off a blood gas because it tells you which direction the primary problem is pushing. Alkalemia is the opposite, a pH above 7.45. Hypercapnia means a high PCO2, which is one possible cause of acidemia but is not the same statement. Hypoxemia refers to low arterial oxygen and is read from PO2, not pH.

cards.q: What term describes an arterial pH above 7.45?
cards.a: Alkalemia.
options: Acidemia
Hypocapnia
Alkalemia
Alkaluria
cards.explanation: Alkalemia is blood that is too alkaline, and it points you toward either a low PCO2 or a high bicarbonate as the cause. Acidemia is the opposite condition. Hypocapnia means a low PCO2, which can produce alkalemia but describes the gas rather than the blood pH. Alkaluria refers to alkaline urine, which is a renal finding and not a statement about arterial blood.

cards.q: Which measured value on a blood gas tells you about the respiratory component of an acid base disorder?
cards.a: PCO2.
options: PCO2
Bicarbonate
pH
PO2
cards.explanation: PCO2 is set by ventilation, so it is the respiratory number on the panel and any primary abnormality in it makes the disorder respiratory. Bicarbonate is the metabolic number, controlled by the kidney and by gains or losses of acid and base. pH tells you the net result but not which system caused it. PO2 reports oxygenation, which is a separate problem from acid base status.

cards.q: Which measured value on a blood gas tells you about the metabolic component of an acid base disorder?
cards.a: Bicarbonate.
options: Bicarbonate
PCO2
PO2
Oxygen saturation
cards.explanation: Bicarbonate reflects the body stores of base and changes with fixed acid gain, base loss, or renal handling, so it is the metabolic number. PCO2 is the respiratory number. PO2 and oxygen saturation both describe oxygen carriage and say nothing directly about acid base balance.

cards.q: In a primary respiratory disorder, how do pH and PCO2 move relative to each other?
cards.a: In opposite directions.
options: In opposite directions
In the same direction
PCO2 changes while pH stays fixed
pH changes while PCO2 stays fixed
cards.explanation: Carbon dioxide is an acid, so a rise in PCO2 lowers pH and a fall in PCO2 raises it, and that opposite movement is the signature of a respiratory problem. Moving in the same direction is the signature of a metabolic problem, where bicarbonate tracks pH. A change in PCO2 always changes pH unless something else is compensating. If pH moved while PCO2 held still, the cause would be metabolic rather than respiratory.

cards.q: In a primary metabolic disorder, how do pH and bicarbonate move relative to each other?
cards.a: In the same direction.
options: In opposite directions
In the same direction
Bicarbonate changes while pH stays fixed
Bicarbonate always stays within its normal range
cards.explanation: Bicarbonate is the base member of the buffer pair, so losing it lowers pH and gaining it raises pH, and that same direction movement marks the disorder as metabolic. Opposite movement is what PCO2 does in a respiratory disorder, which is the distinction students most often collapse. A change in bicarbonate cannot leave pH untouched. Bicarbonate is by definition abnormal in a primary metabolic disorder.

cards.q: What is the name of the disorder in which pH is low and PCO2 is high?
cards.a: Respiratory acidosis.
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
cards.explanation: A high PCO2 means retained carbon dioxide, the acid member of the pair, so it is respiratory and it is an acidosis. Metabolic acidosis also lowers pH but does so through a low bicarbonate with PCO2 normal or low. Respiratory alkalosis has a low PCO2 and a high pH. Metabolic alkalosis has a high bicarbonate and a high pH.

cards.q: What is the name of the disorder in which pH is high and bicarbonate is high?
cards.a: Metabolic alkalosis.
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis
cards.explanation: Bicarbonate is the metabolic number and it has moved in the same direction as pH, so the primary problem is a gain of base or a loss of fixed acid. Respiratory alkalosis raises pH but through a low PCO2, with bicarbonate normal or low. Metabolic acidosis has a low bicarbonate and a low pH. Respiratory acidosis has a high PCO2 and a low pH, and its bicarbonate rises only as compensation.

cards.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.25, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L.
cards.a: Respiratory acidosis.
options: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
cards.explanation: The pH of 7.25 is acidemic, and the PCO2 of 60 mmHg is high, which is the direction that makes blood more acidic, so the respiratory system is the cause. Bicarbonate at 26 mEq/L is at the top of normal and cannot explain an acidemia, so metabolic acidosis is ruled out. Both alkalosis labels are impossible with a pH this low.

cards.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.30, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L.
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis.
options: Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
cards.explanation: The pH of 7.30 is acidemic, PCO2 is exactly normal at 40 mmHg so the lungs are not responsible, and the bicarbonate of 19 mEq/L is low, which is the metabolic cause of the acidemia. Respiratory acidosis would require a PCO2 above 45 mmHg. Neither alkalosis fits a pH below 7.35.

cards.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.55, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L.
cards.a: Metabolic alkalosis.
options: Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
cards.explanation: The pH of 7.55 is alkalemic, PCO2 is normal at 40 mmHg so ventilation is not the cause, and bicarbonate at 34 mEq/L is clearly high, which raises pH and marks the problem as metabolic. Respiratory alkalosis would require a PCO2 below 35 mmHg. Neither acidosis label can accompany a pH above 7.45.

cards.q: Classify this blood gas: pH 7.52, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 22 mEq/L.
cards.a: Respiratory alkalosis.
options: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
cards.explanation: The pH of 7.52 is alkalemic, and the PCO2 of 28 mmHg is low, which removes acid and raises pH, so the cause is respiratory. Bicarbonate at 22 mEq/L is at the low end of normal and could not have raised the pH, so this is not a metabolic alkalosis. Both acidosis labels are ruled out by the high pH.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.14, PCO2 80 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L. Which single value explains the acidemia?
cards.a: The PCO2 of 80 mmHg.
options: Both values together
Neither value, so the sample is in error
The bicarbonate of 26 mEq/L
The PCO2 of 80 mmHg
cards.explanation: Only a value that has moved in the acidifying direction can explain a low pH, and a PCO2 of 80 mmHg is double normal while bicarbonate sits inside its normal range of 22 to 26 mEq/L. A bicarbonate of 26 is if anything faintly alkalinizing, so it cannot be the cause. Calling both responsible ignores that one of them is normal. The set is internally consistent, so there is no reason to suspect a sampling error.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.02, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 10 mEq/L. What does the normal PCO2 tell you?
cards.a: The lungs have not responded to the acidosis.
options: The measurement of pH must be wrong
The disorder must be respiratory in origin
The lungs have not responded to the acidosis
The kidney has fully corrected the disorder
cards.explanation: A severe metabolic acidosis should drive hyperventilation and pull PCO2 well below 40 mmHg, so a normal value here means the expected respiratory response is missing, which is an important warning sign. A normal PCO2 rules the disorder out as respiratory rather than in. A fully corrected disorder would show a pH back near 7.40, not 7.02. The three values are consistent with each other, so the pH is not suspect.

cards.q: A patient loses a large volume of bicarbonate rich intestinal fluid through severe diarrhea. Which disorder develops?
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis.
options: Respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis
cards.explanation: Intestinal secretions are rich in bicarbonate, so losing them strips base from the extracellular fluid, bicarbonate falls, and pH falls with it, which is a metabolic acidosis. Respiratory acidosis would require carbon dioxide retention, and nothing here impairs ventilation. Metabolic alkalosis follows loss of acid, as in vomiting gastric contents, which is the mirror image of this case. Respiratory alkalosis would require hyperventilation as the primary event.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.39, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 32 mEq/L. The pH is inside the normal range. Is there a disorder, and if so which one?
cards.a: Yes, a respiratory acidosis, since pH is on the acid side.
options: Yes, a metabolic alkalosis, since bicarbonate is high
Yes, a mixed disorder, since both values are abnormal here
No, since the pH is within the 7.35 to 7.45 range
Yes, a respiratory acidosis, since pH is on the acid side
cards.explanation: When compensation is complete the pH returns inside the normal range but stops short of 7.40, and the side it lands on identifies the primary problem, so a pH of 7.39 with a high PCO2 and a high bicarbonate is a fully compensated respiratory acidosis. A normal pH alone does not mean normal blood, since both other values are far from normal. Calling it metabolic alkalosis mistakes the compensation for the primary problem, since a primary alkalosis would leave pH above 7.40. In a mixed disorder the two values push pH the same way, and here they oppose each other.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.11, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 17 mEq/L. Why can this not be a simple disorder with compensation?
cards.a: Both values are pushing pH down, so neither one is compensating.
options: The pH is too low for any compensation to have started
Bicarbonate and PCO2 can never be abnormal at the same time
Both values are pushing pH down, so neither is compensating
Compensation never changes bicarbonate, only PCO2
cards.explanation: A high PCO2 acidifies and a low bicarbonate also acidifies, so both a respiratory and a metabolic acidosis are present and there is no compensating move in either direction, which is why this reads as a mixed acidosis. Compensation absolutely does change bicarbonate; that is how the kidney compensates for a respiratory problem. A very low pH does not prevent compensation from starting, and in a simple disorder you would expect to see it. Both values are abnormal at once in every compensated disorder, so that alone is not the problem here.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.60, PCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L. What does the combination indicate?
cards.a: A mixed alkalosis, since a low PCO2 and a high bicarbonate both raise pH.
options: A respiratory alkalosis with full renal compensation
A metabolic alkalosis with full respiratory compensation
A mixed alkalosis, since both values raise pH
A normal result, since the two changes cancel out
cards.explanation: Compensation moves the second value in the same direction as the primary one to blunt the pH change, but here PCO2 has fallen while bicarbonate has risen, so both are driving pH up and the pH is extreme rather than corrected. Renal compensation for a respiratory alkalosis would lower bicarbonate, not raise it. Respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis would raise PCO2, not lower it. The changes reinforce rather than cancel, which is exactly why the pH is 7.60.

cards.q: A patient vomits gastric contents repeatedly for two days, losing hydrochloric acid. Predict bicarbonate and pH, then classify the disorder.
cards.a: Bicarbonate rises, pH rises, and the disorder is a metabolic alkalosis.
options: Bicarbonate rises, pH falls, respiratory acidosis
Bicarbonate falls, pH rises, respiratory alkalosis
Bicarbonate falls, pH falls, metabolic acidosis
Bicarbonate rises, pH rises, metabolic alkalosis
cards.explanation: Every H+ secreted into the stomach leaves a bicarbonate behind in the blood, so removing that acid by vomiting leaves the base unopposed, bicarbonate climbs, and pH rises, which is a metabolic alkalosis. Bicarbonate cannot fall when the acid that would have neutralized it is being discarded. A rising bicarbonate with a falling pH would require a large simultaneous rise in PCO2, which vomiting does not cause. Losing bicarbonate is what happens with diarrhea, from the other end of the gut.

cards.q: What does it mean to call an acid base disorder uncompensated?
cards.a: The system that is not the cause has not yet changed, so its value is still normal.
options: The pH has returned to the normal range
The system that is not the cause is still normal
Both PCO2 and bicarbonate are abnormal
The kidney has excreted all of the excess acid
cards.explanation: Uncompensated means only the primary value has moved, so the other value still sits in its normal range and pH is left fully abnormal. A pH back in the normal range describes full compensation, the opposite situation. Both values abnormal describes partial or full compensation. Full renal excretion of the acid load is correction of the disorder, not compensation for it.

cards.q: What defines a fully compensated acid base disorder?
cards.a: The pH has returned inside 7.35 to 7.45.
options: The pH is back inside 7.35 to 7.45
The pH has settled at exactly 7.40
The primary abnormality has fully resolved
PCO2 and bicarbonate are both back to normal
cards.explanation: Full compensation means the opposing system has pushed pH back inside the normal band, but it has done so by making its own value abnormal, so the panel shows a normal pH with two abnormal numbers. If both values returned to normal the disorder would be gone, not compensated. Compensation stops short of exactly 7.40, which is what lets you identify the primary problem. The primary abnormality persists throughout; that is why compensation is still needed.

cards.q: Which system compensates for a primary metabolic acid base disorder?
cards.a: The respiratory system.
options: The hepatic system
The gastrointestinal system
The respiratory system
The renal system
cards.explanation: A metabolic problem lives in the bicarbonate, so the lungs answer it by adjusting PCO2 within minutes, which is fast but incomplete. The kidney is the compensator for respiratory disorders, not for metabolic ones, and in a metabolic disorder it is often the organ that is failing or being overwhelmed. The liver and gut can cause acid base disturbances but neither is a compensating system.

cards.q: Which system compensates for a primary respiratory acid base disorder?
cards.a: The renal system.
options: The respiratory system
The hepatic system
The renal system
The lymphatic system
cards.explanation: A respiratory problem lives in the PCO2, so the kidney answers it by retaining or dumping bicarbonate over hours to days, which is slow but nearly complete. The respiratory system cannot compensate for itself, since it is the source of the disturbance. The liver handles ammonia and lactate metabolism but is not a compensating organ here, and the lymphatic system plays no acid base role.

cards.q: In a fully compensated disorder, what tells you which system caused the problem?
cards.a: Which side of 7.40 the pH sits on.
options: Which side of 7.40 the pH sits on
Whether PO2 is normal
Whether the bicarbonate is above 24 mEq/L
Which value is further from its normal range
cards.explanation: Compensation brings pH back toward 7.40 but never crosses it, so a compensated pH of 7.37 points to an acidosis and a compensated pH of 7.43 points to an alkalosis, and the abnormal PCO2 or bicarbonate then names the system. Comparing how far each value strays is unreliable, because the compensating change can be large. PO2 reports oxygenation and is silent on acid base cause. A bicarbonate above 24 could be either a primary metabolic alkalosis or renal compensation for a respiratory acidosis.

cards.q: Can compensation carry pH past 7.40 to the opposite side of neutral?
cards.a: No, compensation never overshoots.
options: No, compensation never overshoots
Yes, but only renal compensation does
Yes, but only in the first hour
Yes, routinely, which is how overcorrection happens
cards.explanation: The stimulus for compensating is the abnormal pH itself, so as pH approaches 7.40 the drive fades and the response stops, which is why the compensated pH always stays on the side of the original problem. If a pH were found on the opposite side, the explanation would be a second primary disorder rather than overshoot. That is true for renal and respiratory compensation alike, and it does not change with time.

cards.q: In a partially compensated disorder, what is true of the pH and the two other values?
cards.a: The pH is still outside the normal range and both other values are abnormal.
options: The pH is normal and one other value is abnormal
The pH is abnormal and both other values are abnormal
The pH is abnormal and both other values are normal
The pH is normal and both other values are normal
cards.explanation: Partial compensation means the opposing system has begun to move, so its value has left the normal range, but the response has not been enough to pull pH back inside 7.35 to 7.45. A normal pH with abnormal values is full compensation. An abnormal pH with two normal values is chemically impossible, since something has to explain the pH. All values normal is simply a normal blood gas.

cards.q: During compensation, how does the compensating value move relative to the primary value?
cards.a: In the same direction.
options: In the same direction
It returns toward the middle of its normal range
It stays fixed until the primary value normalizes
In the opposite direction
cards.explanation: If a high PCO2 is the problem, the kidney raises bicarbonate; if a low bicarbonate is the problem, the lungs lower PCO2, so both numbers end up high or both end up low, which restores the ratio that sets pH. Moving in opposite directions would deepen the pH change rather than blunt it, and that pattern signals a mixed disorder. The compensating value leaves the normal range rather than centering itself in it. Waiting for the primary value to normalize would defeat the purpose of compensating.

cards.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.32, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L.
cards.a: Partially compensated.
options: Uncompensated
Partially compensated
Fully compensated
No compensation is possible for this disorder
cards.explanation: The pH of 7.32 is still acidemic, the high PCO2 identifies a respiratory acidosis, and the bicarbonate of 30 mEq/L is above normal, which is the kidney moving in the right direction but not far enough yet. Uncompensated would require a bicarbonate still inside 22 to 26 mEq/L. Full compensation would require the pH back inside 7.35 to 7.45. Renal compensation is very much possible here; it is simply incomplete.

cards.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.37, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L.
cards.a: Fully compensated.
options: Partially compensated
Uncompensated
Overcompensated
Fully compensated
cards.explanation: The pH is back inside the normal range while PCO2 and bicarbonate are both well outside theirs, which is the definition of full compensation, and the pH sitting just below 7.40 confirms the primary problem was an acidosis. Partial compensation would leave pH below 7.35. Uncompensated would leave bicarbonate normal. Overcompensation does not occur, because the drive to compensate disappears as pH nears 7.40.

cards.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.30, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L.
cards.a: Uncompensated.
options: Mixed disorder
Partially compensated
Fully compensated
Uncompensated
cards.explanation: Bicarbonate is low and pH is low, so this is a metabolic acidosis, and the PCO2 of exactly 40 mmHg shows the lungs have not yet responded at all. Partial compensation would require PCO2 below 35 mmHg. Full compensation would require pH back above 7.35. A mixed disorder would need both values pushing pH the same way, but here PCO2 is normal rather than high.

cards.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.50, PCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3- 36 mEq/L.
cards.a: Partially compensated.
options: Fully compensated
Mixed alkalosis
Partially compensated
Uncompensated
cards.explanation: The high bicarbonate with an alkalemic pH marks a metabolic alkalosis, and the PCO2 of 48 mmHg is above normal, meaning ventilation has been reduced to retain acid, which is compensation that has not yet finished. Uncompensated would show a PCO2 in the normal 35 to 45 range. Full compensation would put pH back under 7.45. A mixed alkalosis would require PCO2 to be low, driving pH up further, rather than high.

cards.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.46, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L.
cards.a: Partially compensated.
options: Partially compensated
Uncompensated
Mixed alkalosis
Fully compensated
cards.explanation: The low PCO2 with an alkalemic pH marks a respiratory alkalosis, and the bicarbonate of 19 mEq/L is below normal, which is the kidney dumping base to bring pH down. The pH is still above 7.45, so compensation is incomplete rather than full. Uncompensated would show bicarbonate inside 22 to 26 mEq/L. A mixed alkalosis would require bicarbonate to be high, adding to the alkalemia instead of opposing it.

cards.q: Determine the compensation status: pH 7.37, PCO2 27 mmHg, HCO3- 15 mEq/L.
cards.a: Fully compensated.
options: Mixed acidosis
Uncompensated
Partially compensated
Fully compensated
cards.explanation: The pH has returned inside the normal range while bicarbonate is markedly low and PCO2 is markedly low, which is full compensation, and the pH just under 7.40 identifies the primary problem as a metabolic acidosis. Uncompensated would leave PCO2 near 40 mmHg. Partial compensation would leave pH below 7.35. A mixed acidosis would require PCO2 to be high rather than low.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.33, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 28 mEq/L. Which organ is doing the compensating?
cards.a: The kidney.
options: The lung
The kidney
The liver
No organ, since the disorder is uncompensated
cards.explanation: The high PCO2 with a low pH makes this a respiratory acidosis, so the lung is the source of the problem and the elevated bicarbonate of 28 mEq/L is the kidney retaining base in response. The lung cannot compensate for a disorder it is causing. The liver has no compensating role in acid base balance. Compensation is clearly underway, since bicarbonate has already left the normal range.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.43, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L. Name the primary disorder and the compensating system.
cards.a: A respiratory alkalosis compensated by the kidney.
options: A metabolic alkalosis compensated by the lung
A respiratory acidosis compensated by the kidney
A metabolic acidosis compensated by the lung
A respiratory alkalosis compensated by the kidney
cards.explanation: The pH is normal but sits above 7.40, so the primary problem was an alkalosis, and the low PCO2 is the value that raises pH, making it respiratory, with the low bicarbonate representing renal compensation. A metabolic acidosis would put pH below 7.40 and would be driven by the low bicarbonate instead. A metabolic alkalosis would require a high bicarbonate. A respiratory acidosis would require a high PCO2 and a pH below 7.40.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.44, PCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3- 33 mEq/L. Name the primary disorder and the compensating system.
cards.a: A metabolic alkalosis compensated by the lung.
options: A respiratory acidosis compensated by the kidney
A metabolic acidosis compensated by the lung
A metabolic alkalosis compensated by the lung
A mixed alkalosis with no compensation
cards.explanation: The pH is normal but above 7.40, so the primary problem was an alkalosis, and the high bicarbonate is the value that raises pH, making it metabolic, with the elevated PCO2 showing that ventilation has been reduced to hold acid in. A respiratory acidosis has the same two abnormal values but would leave pH below 7.40, which is why the side of neutral matters so much here. A metabolic acidosis would need a low bicarbonate. A mixed alkalosis would drive pH well above 7.45 rather than back to normal.

cards.q: A patient develops a metabolic acidosis. Compare the blood gas twenty minutes later with the gas three days later.
cards.a: At twenty minutes PCO2 is low with pH still low; by three days pH is near normal.
options: At twenty minutes bicarbonate is already normal; by three days PCO2 has fallen
At twenty minutes PCO2 is low and pH still low; by three days pH is near normal
At twenty minutes nothing has changed at all; by three days PCO2 is low
At twenty minutes pH is already normal; by three days pH has fallen again
cards.explanation: Ventilation responds within minutes, so the early gas shows a low PCO2 that blunts but does not fix the acidemia, and only after two to three days has the kidney excreted the acid load and rebuilt bicarbonate enough to bring pH near normal. Bicarbonate cannot be back to normal in twenty minutes, since renal correction is the slow step. Something has certainly changed by twenty minutes, because chemoreceptors act long before that. The pH does not start normal and then deteriorate in a resolving disorder.

cards.q: A patient has had a stable PCO2 of 60 mmHg for two weeks. Which bicarbonate value fits full renal compensation, and what pH would you expect?
cards.a: About 34 mEq/L, with a pH just under 7.40.
options: About 18 mEq/L, with a pH near 7.10
About 24 mEq/L, with a pH near 7.22
About 34 mEq/L, with a pH just under 7.40
About 34 mEq/L, with a pH just over 7.45
cards.explanation: Two weeks is long enough for full renal compensation, which means bicarbonate rises far enough to restore the ratio and bring pH back inside the normal range but not past 7.40, and a bicarbonate near 34 mEq/L against a PCO2 of 60 mmHg does exactly that. A bicarbonate of 24 mEq/L would mean no compensation at all, leaving pH near 7.22. A pH above 7.45 would be an overshoot, which compensation does not produce. A bicarbonate of 18 mEq/L would push pH lower still and would indicate an added metabolic acidosis.

cards.q: What is the normal range for arterial PO2 in a healthy adult at sea level?
cards.a: 80 to 100 mmHg.
options: 100 to 120 mmHg
35 to 45 mmHg
80 to 100 mmHg
22 to 26 mmHg
cards.explanation: Arterial blood leaving normal lungs carries a PO2 of 80 to 100 mmHg, slightly below alveolar PO2 because of normal shunt and mismatch. The range 35 to 45 mmHg belongs to arterial PCO2. The range 22 to 26 is bicarbonate in mEq/L, not a gas pressure. A PO2 of 100 to 120 mmHg would require supplemental oxygen.

cards.q: What is the normal oxygen saturation of arterial hemoglobin?
cards.a: 95 to 100 percent.
options: 60 to 70 percent
75 to 80 percent
85 to 90 percent
95 to 100 percent
cards.explanation: At a PO2 of 80 to 100 mmHg the blood sits on the flat upper plateau of the oxygen hemoglobin curve, so saturation is 95 percent or better. About 75 percent is the normal saturation of mixed venous blood after tissue extraction. Values of 85 to 90 percent indicate real hypoxemia in arterial blood. Around 60 to 70 percent would be a severe deficit.

cards.q: Which value on a blood gas panel reports oxygenation rather than acid base status?
cards.a: PO2.
options: pH
PO2
PCO2
Bicarbonate
cards.explanation: PO2 describes how well oxygen is being loaded into arterial blood, and a patient can be severely hypoxemic with a perfectly normal pH. PCO2 is a gas but it is the respiratory acid base value, since carbon dioxide becomes carbonic acid. Bicarbonate is the metabolic acid base value. pH is the net acid base result and says nothing about oxygen.

cards.q: How is the bicarbonate value reported on a standard blood gas analyzer obtained?
cards.a: It is calculated from the measured pH and PCO2.
options: It is measured after the sample is centrifuged
It is measured directly with a bicarbonate electrode
It is calculated from the measured pH and PCO2
It is estimated from the hemoglobin concentration
cards.explanation: The analyzer has electrodes for pH, PCO2, and PO2, and it derives bicarbonate from the Henderson Hasselbalch relationship, which is why the three acid base numbers on a gas are always internally consistent. There is no bicarbonate electrode in a standard analyzer. Hemoglobin concentration affects buffering but is not used to compute bicarbonate. Centrifugation separates plasma from cells and is not part of blood gas measurement.

cards.q: An air bubble is left in an arterial blood gas syringe. How does it change the measured values?
cards.a: PO2 is falsely raised and PCO2 is falsely lowered.
options: PO2 is falsely raised and PCO2 falsely lowered
Neither gas changes because the bubble is small
PO2 and PCO2 are both falsely raised
PO2 is falsely lowered and PCO2 falsely raised
cards.explanation: Room air has a PO2 near 160 mmHg and essentially no carbon dioxide, so gases equilibrate across the bubble, pushing the sample PO2 up and its PCO2 down, and the falsely low PCO2 also makes the reported pH too high. Both values cannot rise, since the bubble is high in one gas and empty of the other. The direction cannot be reversed for the same reason. Even a small bubble shifts values enough to change an interpretation.

cards.q: Why must an arterial blood gas sample be analyzed promptly or kept on ice?
cards.a: Blood cells keep metabolizing, consuming oxygen and producing carbon dioxide.
options: Bicarbonate precipitates out of plasma at room temperature
Hemoglobin releases its bound carbon dioxide as the sample warms
Heparin loses its effect within minutes
Blood cells keep metabolizing, using oxygen and making carbon dioxide
cards.explanation: Leukocytes and red blood cells stay alive in the syringe, so a delayed sample shows a falsely low PO2, a falsely high PCO2, and a falsely low pH, and cooling slows that metabolism. Heparin keeps working well beyond the relevant time frame. Bicarbonate stays dissolved and does not precipitate. Hemoglobin does not spontaneously dump carbon dioxide as the sample sits.

cards.q: How does venous blood differ from arterial blood in PCO2 and pH?
cards.a: Venous PCO2 is higher and venous pH is lower.
options: Venous PCO2 is higher and venous pH is lower
Venous PCO2 is lower and venous pH is higher
Both are identical to arterial values
Venous PCO2 is higher and venous pH is also higher
cards.explanation: Tissues add carbon dioxide to blood, so venous PCO2 runs about 6 mmHg above arterial and pH runs roughly 0.03 to 0.05 units lower, which is why an arterial sample is required to judge how well the lungs are working. Venous PCO2 cannot be lower, since carbon dioxide is added on the tissue side. Identical values would mean tissues had produced no carbon dioxide. More carbon dioxide always means a lower pH, not a higher one.

cards.q: Which value should you read first when interpreting a set of arterial blood gas results?
cards.a: The pH.
options: The PCO2
The bicarbonate
The pH
The PO2
cards.explanation: The pH tells you whether the blood is acidemic or alkalemic, and that answer determines which of the other two values could possibly be the cause, so it anchors the whole interpretation. Starting with PCO2 or bicarbonate risks labeling a compensating change as the primary problem. PO2 belongs to the oxygenation question and is read separately.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.33, PCO2 55 mmHg, HCO3- 28 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
cards.a: Long standing airflow obstruction.
options: Two days of vomiting gastric contents
Anxiety with rapid and deep breathing
Long standing airflow obstruction
Three days of profuse watery diarrhea
cards.explanation: The acidemic pH with a high PCO2 makes this a respiratory acidosis, and the raised bicarbonate shows the kidney has had time to begin compensating, which fits long standing airflow obstruction. Anxious hyperventilation lowers PCO2 and would give the opposite picture. Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and produces a metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate. Vomiting loses acid and produces a metabolic alkalosis with a high pH.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.27, PCO2 25 mmHg, HCO3- 11 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
cards.a: Uncontrolled diabetes with ketoacids.
options: Uncontrolled diabetes with ketoacids
Several days of nasogastric suction
A panic attack with hyperventilation
A sedative overdose that slows respiration
cards.explanation: A low pH with a markedly low bicarbonate is a metabolic acidosis, and the low PCO2 is the deep rapid breathing that partially compensates, which is the classic picture when ketoacids accumulate. A sedative overdose raises PCO2 and causes a respiratory acidosis. Nasogastric suction removes gastric acid and causes a metabolic alkalosis with a high pH. A panic attack lowers PCO2 but raises pH, since there is no acid load to explain.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.52, PCO2 44 mmHg, HCO3- 35 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
cards.a: Two days of vomiting gastric contents.
options: A pulmonary embolus causing rapid breathing
Severe diarrhea with bicarbonate loss
Two days of vomiting gastric contents
Opioid induced hypoventilation
cards.explanation: The alkalemic pH with a clearly high bicarbonate and a normal PCO2 is an uncompensated metabolic alkalosis, and losing hydrochloric acid from the stomach leaves bicarbonate unopposed in the blood. A pulmonary embolus drives hyperventilation and produces a respiratory alkalosis with a low PCO2. Diarrhea causes the mirror image, a metabolic acidosis. Opioid hypoventilation raises PCO2 and lowers pH.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.49, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 22 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
cards.a: An acute panic attack with rapid breathing.
options: An acute panic attack with rapid breathing
A week of loop diuretic use
Chronic bronchitis with sputum retention
Renal failure with retained fixed acids
cards.explanation: The alkalemic pH with a low PCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an acute uncompensated respiratory alkalosis, exactly what a burst of hyperventilation produces before the kidney has time to react. Diuretic use causes a metabolic alkalosis, which would show a high bicarbonate. Chronic bronchitis retains carbon dioxide and causes respiratory acidosis. Renal failure retains fixed acid and causes metabolic acidosis with a low bicarbonate.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.14, PCO2 80 mmHg, HCO3- 26 mEq/L. Which cause is most plausible?
cards.a: An opioid overdose that slows breathing.
options: Several days of severe vomiting
An opioid overdose that slows breathing
A drug overdose driving hyperventilation
Ascent to a high mountain altitude
cards.explanation: A very low pH with a PCO2 of 80 mmHg and a normal bicarbonate is an acute uncompensated respiratory acidosis, which means ventilation has abruptly fallen and the kidney has had no time to respond. Altitude drives hyperventilation and lowers PCO2. Vomiting produces a metabolic alkalosis with a high pH. Anything that drives hyperventilation lowers PCO2 rather than doubling it.

cards.q: A patient has had watery diarrhea for three days. Which set of arterial values fits best?
cards.a: pH 7.28, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 14 mEq/L.
options: pH 7.32, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 30 mEq/L
pH 7.46, PCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 19 mEq/L
pH 7.50, PCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3- 36 mEq/L
pH 7.28, PCO2 30 mmHg, HCO3- 14 mEq/L
cards.explanation: Losing bicarbonate rich intestinal fluid lowers plasma bicarbonate and pH, and the low PCO2 shows respiratory compensation already underway, so a low pH with low bicarbonate and low PCO2 is the expected pattern. A pH of 7.50 with a bicarbonate of 36 mEq/L is a metabolic alkalosis, which is what vomiting produces, not diarrhea. A PCO2 of 60 mmHg makes a set a respiratory acidosis, which needs a lung problem rather than a gut one. A pH of 7.46 with a PCO2 of 28 mmHg is a respiratory alkalosis, which diarrhea does not cause.

cards.q: A climber has been at 4200 meters for four days. Which set of arterial values fits best?
cards.a: pH 7.46, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3- 18 mEq/L.
options: pH 7.40, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 24 mEq/L
pH 7.46, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3- 18 mEq/L
pH 7.46, PCO2 50 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L
pH 7.30, PCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3- 12 mEq/L
