cards.explanation: Low inspired oxygen drives hyperventilation, so PCO2 falls and pH rises, and after several days the kidney has excreted bicarbonate to pull pH back toward normal, which gives a mildly alkalemic pH with both PCO2 and bicarbonate low. A PCO2 of 50 mmHg with a bicarbonate of 34 mEq/L is a metabolic alkalosis, and nothing about altitude raises PCO2. A pH of 7.30 is acidemic and would mean an acid load rather than hypoxic hyperventilation. A completely normal set would mean no ventilatory response to altitude at all.

cards.q: A patient in cardiac arrest has a blood gas of pH 7.10, PCO2 60 mmHg, HCO3- 18 mEq/L. Which two processes together explain these numbers?
cards.a: Stopped ventilation plus lactic acid from hypoperfused tissue.
options: Stopped ventilation plus lactic acid from hypoperfused tissue
Hyperventilation plus urinary loss of bicarbonate over hours
Retained carbon dioxide plus renal compensation already underway
Loss of gastric acid plus a reduced rate of ventilation
cards.explanation: The high PCO2 and the low bicarbonate both drive pH down, so there is no compensation here at all and two acidoses are present at once, from stopped ventilation and from anaerobic metabolism in tissue that is not being perfused. Hyperventilation would lower PCO2, not raise it to 60 mmHg. Renal compensation would raise bicarbonate above normal, and it could not act within minutes anyway. Loss of gastric acid raises bicarbonate and would push pH the other way.

cards.q: A patient with a severe asthma attack initially had a PCO2 of 27 mmHg. An hour later it is 42 mmHg while the patient is still working hard to breathe. What has happened to alveolar ventilation and to pH?
cards.a: Alveolar ventilation has fallen and pH has come down toward and below normal.
options: Ventilation has risen further and pH has risen further
Ventilation has fallen and pH has come down toward normal and below
Ventilation is unchanged and pH is unchanged
Ventilation has fallen but pH has risen because bicarbonate rose
cards.explanation: A PCO2 of 27 mmHg means the patient was moving far more air than metabolism required, so a return to 42 mmHg with unchanged carbon dioxide production means alveolar ventilation has dropped, and the accumulating acid pulls pH back down from its alkalemic starting point. Rising ventilation would push PCO2 lower still. Unchanged ventilation cannot produce a fifteen mmHg swing in PCO2. Bicarbonate cannot rise fast enough in an hour to outweigh that carbon dioxide change.

cards.q: A blood gas shows pH 7.48, PCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3- 23 mEq/L, PO2 55 mmHg. Interpret the acid base status and explain what links it to the oxygen value.
cards.a: An uncompensated respiratory alkalosis, driven by hyperventilation in response to the hypoxemia.
options: A metabolic alkalosis, with the low PO2 an unrelated finding
An uncompensated respiratory alkalosis driven by hypoxemic hyperventilation
A fully compensated respiratory acidosis, with hypoxemia from the same lung problem
A mixed alkalosis, with the low PO2 causing bicarbonate retention
cards.explanation: The alkalemic pH with a low PCO2 and a normal bicarbonate is an uncompensated respiratory alkalosis, and the PO2 of 55 mmHg explains it, because low arterial oxygen stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors and drives ventilation, which blows off carbon dioxide. A metabolic alkalosis would require a high bicarbonate. A respiratory acidosis would require a high PCO2 and a pH at or below 7.40. A mixed alkalosis would need bicarbonate to be high, and hypoxemia does not cause the kidney to retain bicarbonate.

cards.q: Two patients both have a PCO2 of 60 mmHg. One has a pH of 7.24 and the other a pH of 7.38. What accounts for the difference?
cards.a: The second has had the disorder long enough for the kidney to raise bicarbonate.
options: The first has a higher PO2, which acidifies the blood
The first has a larger dead space in the lung
The second has a lower rate of carbon dioxide production
The second has had time for the kidney to raise bicarbonate
cards.explanation: pH is set by the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide, so with PCO2 identical the only way to hold pH near normal is a higher bicarbonate, which takes two to three days of renal compensation to build. Carbon dioxide production is not the issue, since PCO2 is already fixed at the same value in both. PO2 does not enter the Henderson Hasselbalch relationship and does not acidify blood. Dead space would change PCO2 itself rather than the pH at a given PCO2.

cards.q: Total body water makes up about what fraction of body weight in a healthy adult?
cards.a: About 60 percent.
options: About 40 percent
About 60 percent
About 80 percent
About 20 percent
cards.explanation: Water is roughly 60 percent of body weight, which is about 42 liters in a 70 kilogram adult and is the starting point for every compartment calculation. About 40 percent is the intracellular share of body weight, not the total. About 20 percent is the extracellular share. Eighty percent would leave almost no room for protein, mineral, and fat.

cards.q: What fraction of total body water is inside cells?
cards.a: About two thirds.
options: About two thirds
About one quarter
About one third
About one half
cards.explanation: Roughly two thirds of body water is intracellular and one third extracellular, so the intracellular compartment is the larger reservoir and absorbs much of any osmotic shift. One third is the extracellular share, which is the value most often swapped in by mistake. One quarter describes plasma as a fraction of extracellular fluid. One half would understate the intracellular volume considerably.

cards.q: Within the extracellular fluid, how is the volume divided between plasma and interstitial fluid?
cards.a: About one quarter plasma and three quarters interstitial.
options: About three quarters plasma and one quarter interstitial
Almost all plasma, with very little interstitial fluid
About one quarter plasma and three quarters interstitial
About half and half
cards.explanation: Of roughly 14 liters of extracellular fluid, about 3 liters is plasma and about 11 liters bathes the tissues, which is why a loss confined to plasma is a small share of extracellular volume. An even split would overstate the vascular compartment. Reversing the ratio would give a plasma volume that the heart could not accommodate. Interstitial fluid is by far the larger of the two.

cards.q: What is the normal osmolarity of body fluids?
cards.a: About 290 mOsm/L.
options: About 1200 mOsm/L
About 150 mOsm/L
About 290 mOsm/L
About 400 mOsm/L
cards.explanation: Plasma and intracellular fluid both sit near 290 mOsm/L, and because water crosses cell membranes freely the two compartments always end at the same osmolarity. About 150 mOsm/L would be severely dilute. Around 400 mOsm/L is markedly concentrated. About 1200 mOsm/L is the maximum concentration of urine, not of body fluid.

cards.q: Which solute is the main determinant of extracellular fluid osmolarity?
cards.a: Sodium with its accompanying anions.
options: Glucose
Potassium with its accompanying anions
Sodium with its accompanying anions
Plasma albumin
cards.explanation: Sodium and the chloride and bicarbonate that follow it account for most extracellular particles, which is why plasma sodium concentration is the practical readout of extracellular osmolarity. Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation and is present in plasma at only about 4 mEq/L. Albumin has a large mass but very few particles, so it contributes almost nothing to osmolarity even though it sets colloid osmotic pressure. Glucose adds a small share that only becomes important when it rises far above normal.

cards.q: Which ion is the major cation of intracellular fluid?
cards.a: Potassium.
options: Magnesium
Sodium
Calcium
Potassium
cards.explanation: Potassium is held at roughly 140 mEq/L inside cells by the Na+/K+ ATPase, and it is the counterpart to sodium outside. Sodium is the major extracellular cation and is kept low inside. Free intracellular calcium is measured in nanomolar amounts because it acts as a signal. Magnesium is present intracellularly but at far lower concentration than potassium.

cards.q: What is the difference between the osmolarity of a solution and its tonicity?
cards.a: Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the cell membrane.
options: Osmolarity applies to plasma and tonicity to interstitial fluid
Tonicity counts only solutes that cannot cross the membrane
Tonicity counts only charged solutes
Osmolarity is measured at 37 C and tonicity at room temperature
cards.explanation: Tonicity describes what a solution does to cell volume, so only impermeant solutes count, which is why a urea solution can be isosmotic yet hypotonic as urea equilibrates and water follows into the cell. Charge is irrelevant, since glucose is uncharged and still contributes fully to tonicity. Temperature is not what separates the two terms. Both terms apply to any fluid, not to particular compartments.

cards.q: What drives water movement between the intracellular and extracellular compartments?
cards.a: The osmotic gradient across the cell membrane.
options: The colloid osmotic pressure of albumin
Hydrostatic pressure across the cell membrane
The osmotic gradient across the cell membrane
Active pumping of water by the Na+/K+ ATPase
cards.explanation: Water moves toward the compartment with the higher osmolarity until the two are equal, and cell membranes cannot sustain a pressure difference, so osmosis alone sets the distribution. Hydrostatic pressure drives filtration across capillary walls, which is a different boundary. There is no water pump; the sodium pump moves solute and water follows. Albumin governs the split between plasma and interstitial fluid, not the split across the cell membrane.

cards.q: One liter of isotonic saline is infused. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
cards.a: Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift into or out of cells.
options: Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift across the cell membrane
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no shift across the cell membrane
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
cards.explanation: Isotonic saline has the same effective osmolarity as body fluid, so it stays where it is put, expanding the extracellular compartment while osmolarity and cell volume are unchanged. Water would enter cells only if extracellular osmolarity had fallen. Water would leave cells only if extracellular osmolarity had risen. Adding fluid is expansion, so depletion is ruled out at the start.

cards.q: A person drinks two liters of plain water. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
cards.a: Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells.
options: Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
cards.explanation: Pure water adds volume without solute, so extracellular osmolarity falls below intracellular, water crosses into cells, and both compartments end larger and more dilute. An isosmotic result would require the added fluid to carry solute at 290 mOsm/L. Water cannot leave cells when the outside has become more dilute. Drinking adds volume, so this cannot be depletion.

cards.q: One liter of hypertonic saline is infused. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
cards.a: Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
cards.explanation: Concentrated salt raises extracellular osmolarity, so water is pulled out of cells, and the extracellular compartment grows by more than the volume infused while cells shrink. Water moves into cells only when the outside is more dilute. An isosmotic result would need the infusion to match body osmolarity. Total body volume rises here, so this is expansion rather than depletion.

cards.q: An athlete sweats heavily for three hours and drinks nothing. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
cards.a: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with water leaving cells
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no shift
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
cards.explanation: Sweat is hypotonic, so more water than salt is lost, extracellular osmolarity climbs while extracellular volume falls, and water is drawn out of cells so both compartments shrink. An isosmotic loss would require sweat to match plasma osmolarity, which it does not. Water cannot enter cells when the outside has become more concentrated. Losing fluid is depletion, not expansion.

cards.q: A patient loses two liters of blood through hemorrhage. Classify the disturbance and predict the immediate fluid shift across cell membranes.
cards.a: Isosmotic volume depletion, with no immediate shift.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no shift
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no immediate shift
cards.explanation: Whole blood is lost at the osmolarity of body fluid, so the extracellular compartment shrinks while osmolarity stays at 290 mOsm/L and cells are initially untouched. A hyperosmotic result would require losing relatively more water than solute, as in sweating. A hypoosmotic result would require losing relatively more solute than water. Losing volume is depletion, so expansion is ruled out.

cards.q: A patient with too little aldosterone loses sodium in the urine while water intake continues. Classify the disturbance and predict the fluid shift.
cards.a: Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells.
options: Hyperosmotic volume depletion, with water leaving cells
Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with water entering cells
Isosmotic volume depletion, with no shift
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with water entering cells
cards.explanation: Losing sodium without an equal loss of water lowers extracellular osmolarity, so the extracellular compartment shrinks from the salt loss while water shifts into cells and makes that shrinkage worse. A hyperosmotic result would require water loss to exceed solute loss, the opposite of what happens here. An isosmotic loss would leave osmolarity at 290 mOsm/L. Extracellular volume falls, so this is depletion rather than expansion.

cards.q: A marathon runner sweats heavily and then drinks four liters of plain water. Trace extracellular osmolarity and cell volume across the two events.
cards.a: Osmolarity rises with sweating and then falls below normal after drinking, so cells first shrink and then swell.
options: Osmolarity rises then falls, so cells first shrink and then swell
Osmolarity rises in both phases, so cells shrink throughout
Osmolarity stays at 290 mOsm/L throughout, so cell volume never changes
Osmolarity falls then rises, so cells first swell and then shrink
cards.explanation: Hypotonic sweat concentrates the extracellular fluid and pulls water out of cells, and then replacing the losses with water alone dilutes the remaining solute below normal so water moves back into cells and past their starting volume, which is how exercise associated hyponatremia produces cerebral swelling. The order cannot be reversed, since sweating comes first. Osmolarity cannot keep rising once large volumes of pure water are added. It cannot stay fixed while solute free water is both lost and replaced.

cards.q: A patient secretes too much antidiuretic hormone and retains water while sodium excretion continues normally. Classify the disturbance and predict what happens to cell volume.
cards.a: Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with cells swelling.
options: Hypoosmotic volume depletion, with cells swelling
Isosmotic volume expansion, with no change in cell volume
Hyperosmotic volume expansion, with cells shrinking
Hypoosmotic volume expansion, with cells swelling
cards.explanation: Retaining solute free water adds volume while diluting the solute already present, so osmolarity falls, water follows into cells, and every compartment ends larger and more dilute, which is why plasma sodium is low in this condition. Cells cannot shrink when the fluid around them is dilute. Total volume rises, so this is expansion, not depletion. An isosmotic result would require sodium to be retained in proportion to the water.

cards.q: Two patients have each lost three liters of fluid, one through hemorrhage and one through pure water loss. Which lost more intracellular volume, and why?
cards.a: The water loss patient, since osmolarity rose.
options: The hemorrhage patient, because plasma volume fell fastest
The water loss patient, since osmolarity rose
Both lost the same, because total body water fell equally
Neither lost intracellular volume, because cells are protected
cards.explanation: Hemorrhage removes fluid at body osmolarity, so the loss stays extracellular and cells are spared, while pure water loss concentrates the extracellular fluid and drags water out of every cell, spreading the deficit across both compartments. Speed of plasma loss does not determine where the deficit ends up; osmolarity does. Equal total losses do not mean equal distribution, which is exactly the point of the comparison. Cells are not protected from osmotic gradients at all.

cards.q: A hyperosmotic, volume depleted patient absorbs three liters of solute free water from the gut. Roughly how does that water distribute, and what does that mean for the extracellular deficit?
cards.a: About two liters enter cells and one stays outside.
options: All three liters stay extracellular, filling the deficit completely
About two liters enter cells and one stays outside
All three liters enter cells, leaving the deficit unchanged
The water enters plasma alone, raising blood volume by three liters
cards.explanation: Solute free water follows the osmotic gradient until both compartments match, and since roughly two thirds of body water is intracellular, about two thirds of the added water ends up inside cells, so osmolarity is corrected far more effectively than volume. Water cannot stay entirely extracellular, because nothing holds it there once osmolarity falls. It cannot all enter cells either, since the shift stops when the two compartments are equal. Confining it to plasma would ignore the interstitial space, which is roughly three times larger than plasma.
